newsitem.title: CANADA: Canada's wheat seen blocked by rail rate cap.
newsitem.headline: Canada's wheat seen blocked by rail rate cap.

text.p: Legislated caps on rail rates for grain shipments are keeping wheat on Canada's Prairies while ocean vessels wait for it on the Pacific coast, grain and transportation analysts said Tuesday.
"It's a comedy of errors that comes down to profits," one grain industry analyst said. "It's more profitable to haul other commodities because of the cap on grain rates."

On Tuesday 42 ocean vessels were waiting to load grain on the Pacific coast, including 12 destined for Japan. Some had been waiting as long as 39 days. Another 13 ships were due to arrive later this week.
Rail rates on grain cannot exceed a federally mandated cap, while other commodities without such restrictions may be getting priority over grain, transportation industry analysts said.

The Canadian Wheat Board has already deferred shipment of more than 1.5 million tonnes of grain since early January because of the rail shipment delays. The Wheat Board faces demurrage fines of more than C$15 million along with lost sales up to April.
The Wheat Board charged last week that grain was a low priority for the railways.
"When the system's tight it amplifies problems," an analyst said. "You don't have the engine power to go around, so it goes to the highest paying commodity and that's not grain."
The Canadian government is due to review the grain rail rate cap and perhaps even the necessity for one in 1999.
"I heard the Japanese are already crying," another analyst said. "We don't look like a reliable supplier. Farmers lose, grain companies lose and the railways lose."
Canadian Agriculture Minister Ralph Goodale on Tuesday told Parliament the railways assured him more locomotives would be assigned to move grain to ports from the Prairies.
The Saskatchewan Wheat Pool, Canada's largest grain handler, on Tuesday asked Goodale to convene an emergency meeting to solve the crisis.
